Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Some bots misbehave: they flood rooms, or their webhooks keep failing.

> As an administrator, I want misbehaving bots to be stopped automatically,
> and I want to decide when they come back.

Flooding:

- A bot may post at most 10 messages in any 10 seconds. Messages posted through the API and webhook replies both count.
- The message that goes over the limit is rejected and starts a 30-second cooldown. During the cooldown, the posting endpoint responds with `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header (seconds left), and webhook replies are not posted.
- Five more attempts to post during the same cooldown suspend the bot.

Failing webhooks:

- A failed delivery is any response other than `2xx`, a timeout, or a connection error.
- Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend the bot. A successful delivery resets the count.

A suspended bot:

- gets `403 Forbidden` from the posting endpoint;
- receives no webhooks;
- keeps its rooms and messages, and still counts towards its owner's bot limit;
- stays listed on the bots page and shows as "Suspended", with the reason.

Only administrators can reactivate a suspended bot, from the bots page: a "Reactivate" button that asks for confirmation. The limits above are fixed in code; they have no settings.

# Campfire

Campfire is a web-based chat application. It supports many of the features you'd
expect, including:

- Multiple rooms, with access controls
- Direct messages
- File attachments with previews
- Search
- Notifications (via Web Push)
- Chat bots that post messages over HTTP, and that get a webhook when they're mentioned or join a room (see [bots](docs/bots.md))
- @mentions

## Running your own Campfire instance

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional,
single-machine deployment. This includes the web app, background jobs, caching,
file serving, and SSL. You can use our pre-built image at
`ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, or build your own from this repo.

### Deploying with ONCE

The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).
It will guide you through the initial set up and then keep your instance up to date automatically.

If you don't already have `once` installed, run this on the machine you want to run Campfire on:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com | sh
```

`once` will launch as soon as the install is finished. 

Choose Campfire from the list of applications, follow the instructions, and ONCE will take care of the rest.

If you prefer the command line to the dashboard, you can deploy directly:

```sh
once deploy ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire --host chat.example.com
```

### Deploying with Docker

If you'd rather run the Docker image yourself, you can read more about that in the [self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md).

> [!TIP]
> When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through a wizard to create an admin account.
> The email address that you enter for the admin account will be visible on the sign-in page, it's there so
> that people have someone to contact if they need help with their account. If that bothers you, put in any
> email address you want and create yourself a new admin account.

## Development

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
Please see our [development guide](docs/development.md) for how to get Campfire set up for local development.

## Security

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for how to report a vulnerability and a description of our trust model.

# Campfire

Campfire is a web-based chat application. It supports many of the features you'd
expect, including:

- Multiple rooms, with access controls
- Direct messages
- File attachments with previews
- Search
- Notifications (via Web Push)
- Chat bots that post messages over HTTP, and that get a webhook when they're mentioned or join a room (see [bots](docs/bots.md))
- @mentions

## Running your own Campfire instance

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional,
single-machine deployment. This includes the web app, background jobs, caching,
file serving, and SSL. You can use our pre-built image at
`ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, or build your own from this repo.

### Deploying with ONCE

The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).
It will guide you through the initial set up and then keep your instance up to date automatically.

If you don't already have `once` installed, run this on the machine you want to run Campfire on:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com | sh
```

`once` will launch as soon as the install is finished. 

Choose Campfire from the list of applications, follow the instructions, and ONCE will take care of the rest.

If you prefer the command line to the dashboard, you can deploy directly:

```sh
once deploy ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire --host chat.example.com
```

### Deploying with Docker

If you'd rather run the Docker image yourself, you can read more about that in the [self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md).

> [!TIP]
> When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through a wizard to create an admin account.
> The email address that you enter for the admin account will be visible on the sign-in page, it's there so
> that people have someone to contact if they need help with their account. If that bothers you, put in any
> email address you want and create yourself a new admin account.

## Development

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
Please see our [development guide](docs/development.md) for how to get Campfire set up for local development.

## Security

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for how to report a vulnerability and a description of our trust model.

**Who joins open rooms.** People are granted every open room when they are created (`User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms`,
which skips bots). A bot gets open rooms only through its switch, a boolean column on `bots` (`join_all_open_rooms`,
default off). `Bot#join_open_rooms` runs in the save that turns the switch on, and `Rooms::Open` grants a new open room
to `User.joining_open_rooms`: people, plus the bots whose switch is on.

**Fetching webhooks** uses `RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard`, as link unfurling does (see `SECURITY.md`: any member
can make Campfire fetch a URL, so the destination is checked). The checked address is pinned with `ipaddr:`, so a DNS
change between the check and the connection can't move the request to an internal host. Redirects aren't followed,
the body is read only up to 64 KB, and a `Timeout` caps the whole exchange, so a bot can't keep a worker busy by
dripping bytes slowly.

**Answers from bots** go through the same sanitizing filters the room uses on display
(`ContentFilters::SanitizeTags` and `SanitizeAttributes`) before they're stored, and all `action-text-attachment`
elements are removed first. An attachment in a bot's answer would notify the person it names as if they had written
it, so bots can't create mentions.

**The bot code in the payload.** `room.reply_to` contains the bot code, so the webhook's recipient learns it. That's
intended: the webhook is the bot. Apart from the bots page, that's the only place the code leaves Campfire, and the payload is never logged.

**Webhook URLs are secrets** (they often carry a token in the path or query). The parameter filter masks
`webhook_url` in request logs and in `inspect`, and the bot's edit page isn't cached.

**Authorization.** Editing and deleting use `Current.user.can_administer?(bot)`, which means administrator or
creator, the same rule used for other records here.

## Protecting bot codes

A bot code grants the ability to post as the bot, so:

- It's shown only on `/bots`, to the bot's creator and administrators. The edit page doesn't show it.
- `/bots` is served with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `turbo-cache-control: no-cache`, so neither the browser nor
  Turbo's page cache keeps a copy.
- It never appears in messages, broadcasts, redirects, flash messages or JSON. The one exception is `room.reply_to`
  in a webhook payload, which goes only to that bot's own webhook (see "Receiving mentions").
- Rails' parameter filter masks it (`bot_key` matches the existing `_key` filter), so `Parameters:` log lines show
  `[FILTERED]`.
- Rails masks only the query string when it logs a path, so `lib/rails_ext/filtered_bot_path.rb` masks the code in
  the path too: `Started POST "/rooms/1/[FILTERED]/messages"`. `Bot.filter_path` does the same for Sentry request
  URLs (`config/initializers/sentry.rb`).
- The code is generated by `has_secure_token` (24 base58 characters, about 140 bits) and is unique in the database.

Known limits:

- The code is stored in plain text, because the page has to show it again. Anyone with database access can read it.
- ActiveRecord's SQL debug logging prints the value in the `bots.bot_key` query, in development or with
  `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. Session tokens already appear the same way. Production logs at `info` by default.
- Reverse-proxy access logs record the full path, which includes the code. Treat those logs as sensitive.

Not built yet: rotating a bot code (`regenerate_bot_key` is available), rate limiting failed code attempts,
per-bot scopes, and a size limit on message bodies (any size is accepted today).

Known limits (webhooks):

- Private and internal webhook addresses are refused, so a bot whose service runs on the same private network as
  Campfire can't use a webhook yet. Allowing them would be a deliberate, per-deployment decision.
- Requests aren't signed, so the webhook URL is the only secret. A receiver can't tell a genuine mention from a
  forged POST unless the URL is secret.
- There are no retries and no delivery log. A failed webhook is only logged, by class.
- Sentry's HTTP breadcrumbs record a webhook's scheme, host and path (not its query) when an error is reported after a
  webhook call. They go to the operator's own `SENTRY_DSN`.

# The bot message API. A bot posts by sending the message text as the raw request body, e.g.
#
#   curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-key>/messages
#
# There is no session here: the bot key in the path is the credential.
class Bots::MessagesController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access
  skip_forgery_protection

  before_action :set_bot, :set_room

  rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound do
    head :not_found
  end

  def create
    text = message_text
    return head :unprocessable_content unless text

    @message = @bot.post_text(@room, text)

    head :created, location: message_path(@message)
  end

  # Clients send curl's default form encoding, and Rails would try to parse the body as form fields before the
  # action runs, rejecting text such as "100% done". The body is the message, so it's never read as fields.
  def process_action(...)
    request.request_parameters = {}
    super
  end

  private
    def set_bot
      @bot = Bot.active.find_by(bot_key: params[:bot_key])

      unless @bot
        response.headers["WWW-Authenticate"] = %(Bot realm="Campfire")
        head :unauthorized
      end
    end

    def set_room
      @room = @bot.user.rooms.find(params[:room_id])
    end

    # The body as text, stripped. Nil when it's blank or isn't valid UTF-8, which both count as an empty message.
    def message_text
      text = String.new(request.raw_post, encoding: Encoding::UTF_8)
      text.strip if text.valid_encoding? && text.present?
    end
end

class BotsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_bot, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_create, only: %i[ new create ]

  def index
    # The page shows bot keys, so neither the browser nor anything in between should keep a copy.
    response.cache_control.merge!(no_store: true)

    @bots = (Current.user.can_administer? ? Bot.all : Bot.created_by(Current.user)).ordered.preload(:user)
  end

  def new
    @bot = Bot.new
  end

  def create
    Bot.create!(bot_params)

    redirect_to bots_url, notice: "✓"
  end

  def edit
    # The page shows the webhook URL, which can carry a secret of its own, so it's kept out of caches too.
    response.cache_control.merge!(no_store: true)
  end

  def update
    @bot.update!(bot_params)

    redirect_to bots_url, notice: "✓"
  end

  def destroy
    @bot.deactivate

    redirect_to bots_url
  end

  private
    def set_bot
      @bot = Bot.find(params[:id])
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@bot)
    end

    # A member at the limit can't reach the form or post a bot, whatever the bots page offers. The page says why.
    def ensure_can_create
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_create_bot?
    end

    # Browsers send an empty avatar field when no file was picked, which mustn't clear the existing avatar. An empty
    # webhook URL does clear it, so that's left alone. The switch's hidden field sends false when it's off, so a form
    # always says which it is; a request that leaves the field out leaves the switch as it was.
    def bot_params
      params.require(:bot).permit(:name, :avatar, :webhook_url, :join_all_open_rooms).compact
    end
end

      room = proxy_association.owner

      destroy_by user: users
    end

      transaction do

        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end

  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

      order(:created_at).first
    end

      end

    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end

    def ask_mentioned_bots_later(message)

    end

  "output": "class MessagesController < ApplicationController
  include ActiveStorage::SetCurrent, RoomScoped

  before_action :set_room, except: :create
  before_action :set_message, only: %i[ show edit update destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]

  layout false, only: :index

  def index
    @messages = find_paged_messages

    if @messages.any?
      fresh_when @messages
    else
      head :no_content
    end
  end

  def create
    set_room
    @message = @room.messages.create_with_attachment!(message_params)

    @message.broadcast_create
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound
    render action: :room_not_found
  end

  def show
  end

  def edit
  end

  def update
    @message.update!(message_params)

    @message.broadcast_replace_to @room, :messages, target: [ @message, :presentation ], partial: "messages/presentation", attributes: { maintain_scroll: true }

    redirect_to room_message_url(@room, @message)
  end

  def destroy
    @message.destroy
    @message.broadcast_remove
  end

  private
    def set_message
      @message = @room.messages.find(params[:id])
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@message)
    end


    def find_paged_messages
      case
      when params[:before].present?
        @room.messages.with_creator.page_before(@room.messages.find(params[:before]))
      when params[:after].present?
        @room.messages.with_creator.page_after(@room.messages.find(params[:after]))
      else
        @room.messages.with_creator.last_page
      end
    end


    def message_params
      params.require(:message).permit(:body, :attachment, :client_message_id)
    end
end

class Message < ApplicationRecord
  include Attachment, Broadcasts, Mentionee, Pagination, Searchable

  belongs_to :room, touch: true
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy

  has_rich_text :body

  before_create -> { self.client_message_id ||= Random.uuid }
  after_create_commit -> { room.receive(self) }

  scope :ordered, -> { order(:created_at) }
  scope :with_creator, -> { preload(creator: :avatar_attachment) }
  scope :with_attachment_details, -> {
    with_rich_text_body_and_embeds
    with_attached_attachment
      .includes(attachment_blob: :variant_records)
  }
  scope :with_boosts, -> { includes(boosts: :booster) }

  def plain_text_body
    body.to_plain_text.presence || attachment&.filename&.to_s || ""
  end

  def to_key
    [ client_message_id ]
  end

  def content_type
    case
    when attachment?    then "attachment"
    when sound.present? then "sound"
    else                     "text"
    end.inquiry
  end

  def sound
    plain_text_body.match(/\A\/play (?<name>\w+)\z/) do |match|
      Sound.find_by_name match[:name]
    end
  end
end

class Account < ApplicationRecord
  include Joinable

  has_one_attached :logo do |attachable|
    attachable.variant :large, resize_to_limit: [ 512, 512 ], format: :png
    attachable.variant :small, resize_to_limit: [ 192, 192 ], format: :png
  end

  # bots_per_member caps how many bots each member can have. Administrators aren't limited by it.
  has_json :settings, restrict_room_creation_to_administrators: false, bots_per_member: 5

  validate :bots_per_member_must_be_a_count

  def logo_variant(size)
    logo.variant(size).processed if logo.variable?
  end

  private
    # Blank input is cast to nil, and a negative count would never let anyone create a bot, so both are refused.
    # Messages are strings: with a symbol type, Rails reads the attribute from this record to build the message, and
    # Account has no bots_per_member method to answer it.
    def bots_per_member_must_be_a_count
      limit = settings.bots_per_member

      if limit.nil?
        errors.add :bots_per_member, "can't be blank"
      elsif limit < 0
        errors.add :bots_per_member, "must be zero or more"
      end
    end
end

  before_action :set_room, except: :create
  before_action :set_message, only: %i[ show edit update destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]

  layout false, only: :index

  def index
    @messages = find_paged_messages

    if @messages.any?
      fresh_when @messages
    else
      head :no_content
    end
  end

  def create
    set_room
    @message = @room.messages.create_with_attachment!(message_params)

    @message.broadcast_create
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound
    render action: :room_not_found
  end

  def show
  end

  def edit
  end

  def update
    @message.update!(message_params)

    @message.broadcast_replace_to @room, :messages, target: [ @message, :presentation ], partial: "messages/presentation", attributes: { maintain_scroll: true }

    redirect_to room_message_url(@room, @message)
  end

  def destroy
    @message.destroy
    @message.broadcast_remove
  end

  private
    def set_message
      @message = @room.messages.find(params[:id])
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@message)
    end


    def find_paged_messages
      case
      when params[:before].present?
        @room.messages.with_creator.page_before(@room.messages.find(params[:before]))
      when params[:after].present?
        @room.messages.with_creator.page_after(@room.messages.find(params[:after]))
      else
        @room.messages.with_creator.last_page
      end
    end


    def message_params
      params.require(:message).permit(:body, :attachment, :client_message_id)
    end
end

class Message < ApplicationRecord
  include Attachment, Broadcasts, Mentionee, Pagination, Searchable

  belongs_to :room, touch: true
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy

  has_rich_text :body

  before_create -> { self.client_message_id ||= Random.uuid }
  after_create_commit -> { room.receive(self) }

  scope :ordered, -> { order(:created_at) }
  scope :with_creator, -> { preload(creator: :avatar_attachment) }
  scope :with_attachment_details, -> {
    with_rich_text_body_and_embeds
    with_attached_attachment
      .includes(attachment_blob: :variant_records)
  }
  scope :with_boosts, -> { includes(boosts: :booster) }

  def plain_text_body
    body.to_plain_text.presence || attachment&.filename&.to_s || ""
  end

  def to_key
    [ client_message_id ]
  end

  def content_type
    case
    when attachment?    then "attachment"
    when sound.present? then "sound"
    else                     "text"
    end.inquiry
  end

  def sound
    plain_text_body.match(/\A\/play (?<name>\w+)\z/) do |match|
      Sound.find_by_name match[:name]
    end
  end
end

class Account < ApplicationRecord
  include Joinable

  has_one_attached :logo do |attachable|
    attachable.variant :large, resize_to_limit: [ 512, 512 ], format: :png
    attachable.variant :small, resize_to_limit: [ 192, 192 ], format: :png
  end

  # bots_per_member caps how many bots each member can have. Administrators aren't limited by it.
  has_json :settings, restrict_room_creation_to_administrators: false, bots_per_member: 5

  validate :bots_per_member_must_be_a_count

  def logo_variant(size)
    logo.variant(size).processed if logo.variable?
  end

  private
    # Blank input is cast to nil, and a negative count would never let anyone create a bot, so both are refused.
    # Messages are strings: with a symbol type, Rails reads the attribute from this record to build the message, and
    # Account has no bots_per_member method to answer it.
    def bots_per_member_must_be_a_count
      limit = settings.bots_per_member

      if limit.nil?
        errors.add :bots_per_member, "can't be blank"
      elsif limit < 0
        errors.add :bots_per_member, "must be zero or more"
      end
    end
end

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end

    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload

        build_shared_payload

# Rooms open to all users on the account. When a new user is added to the account, they're automatically granted membership.
# Bots are the exception: they're granted membership only when they're set to join all open rooms.
class Rooms::Open < Room
  after_save_commit :grant_access_to_all_users

  private
    def grant_access_to_all_users
      memberships.grant_to(User.active.joining_open_rooms) if type_previously_changed?(to: "Rooms::Open")
    end
end

class Membership < ApplicationRecord
  include Connectable

  belongs_to :room
  belongs_to :user

  after_destroy_commit { user.reset_remote_connections }

  enum :involvement, %w[ invisible nothing mentions everything ].index_by(&:itself), prefix: :involved_in

  scope :with_ordered_room, -> { includes(:room).joins(:room).order("LOWER(rooms.name)") }
  scope :without_direct_rooms, -> { joins(:room).where.not(room: { type: "Rooms::Direct" }) }

  scope :visible, -> { where.not(involvement: :invisible) }
  scope :unread,  -> { where.not(unread_at: nil) }

  def read
    update!(unread_at: nil)
  end

  def unread?
    unread_at.present?
  end
end

require "test_helper"

class BotsControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  include ActionView::RecordIdentifier

  setup do
    sign_in :david
    @bot = Bot.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:david))
  end

  test "index lists the bots you created with their name and bot code" do
    get bots_url

    assert_response :success
    assert_select "#bots li##{dom_id(@bot)}" do
      assert_select "strong", text: "Deploy Bot"
      assert_select "label[for=?]", dom_id(@bot, :bot_key), text: "Bot code"
      assert_select "input[id=?][readonly][value=?]", dom_id(@bot, :bot_key), @bot.bot_key
    end
  end

  test "index shows every bot on one page, without pagination" do
    12.times { |i| Bot.create!(name: "Bot #{i}", creator: users(:david)) }

    get bots_url

    assert_select "#bots li", count: 13
    assert_select "turbo-frame#next_page_container", count: 0
  end

  test "index doesn't list or expose bots created by someone else" do
    sign_in :kevin # a member, rather than an administrator who sees every bot
    get bots_url

    assert_select "strong", text: "Deploy Bot", count: 0
    assert_not_includes response.body, @bot.bot_key
  end

  test "administrators see every bot" do
    other = Bot.create!(name: "Someone Else's Bot", creator: users(:jz))

    sign_in :jason
    get bots_url

    assert_select "strong", text: "Deploy Bot"
    assert_select "strong", text: "Someone Else's Bot"
    assert_includes response.body, other.bot_key
  end

    end

  include ActiveStorage::Streaming

  rescue_from(ActiveSupport::MessageVerifier::InvalidSignature) { head :not_found }

  def show
    @user = User.from_avatar_token(params[:user_id])

    if stale?(etag: @user)

# How to contribute to Campfire

Campfire uses GitHub
[discussions](https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/discussions) to track
feature requests and questions, rather than [the issue
tracker](https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/issues). If you're considering
opening an issue or pull request, please open a discussion instead.

Whenever a discussion leads to an actionable and well-understood task, we'll
move it to the issue tracker where it can be worked on.

This is a little different than how some other projects work, but it makes it
easier for us to triage and prioritise the work. It also means that the open
issues all represent agreed-upon tasks that are either being worked on, or are
ready to be worked on.

This should also make it easier to see what's in progress, and to find
something to work on if you'd like to do so.

## What this means in practice

### If you'd like to contribute to the code...

1. If you're interested in working on one of the open issues, please do! We are
   grateful for the help!
2. You'll want to make sure someone else isn't already working on the same
   issue. If they are, it will be tagged "in progress" and/or it should be clear
   from the comments. When in doubt, you can always comment on the issue to ask.
3. Similarly, if you need any help or guidance on the issue, please comment on
   the issue as you go, and we'll do our best to help.
4. When you have something ready for review or collaboration, open a PR.

### If you've found a bug...

1. If you don't have steps to reproduce the problem, or you're not certain it's a
   bug, open a discussion.
2. If you have steps to reproduce, open an issue.

### If you have an idea for a feature...

1. Open a discussion.

### If you have a question, or are having trouble with configuration...

1. Open a discussion.

Hopefully this process makes it easier for everyone to be involved. Thanks for
helping! ❤️

"
}

messages.content:
I have enough context to settle the design. Summary of the plan:

- **State lives on `bots`**: suspension (`suspended_at`, `suspension_reason`), the consecutive webhook failure count, and the cooldown (`cooldown_until`, `cooldown_attempts`).
- **Flood window is counted from the bot's `messages` rows** (API posts and webhook replies both create messages), so there's no second source of truth.
- **Posting goes through one choke point** (`Bot::Throttle`) that runs inside `with_lock`, so check-then-insert is serialized. State is committed before a refusal is raised, so refused attempts still count.
- **Webhook outcomes** are recorded in the delivery job: any 2xx resets the counter; non-2xx, timeouts, and connection errors increment it.
- **Suspended bots** are excluded at enqueue time and at delivery time, and reactivation is an admin-only `POST` with a `turbo_confirm` button.

I'll start with the migration.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > app/models/bot/suspendable.rb <<'EOF'
# A suspended bot can't post and gets no webhooks, but it keeps its rooms and messages, and it still counts towards its
# owner's bot limit. Suspension comes from flooding (see Bot::Throttle) or from a webhook that keeps failing, which is
# counted here. Only administrators reactivate a bot (see Bots::ReactivationsController), so a bot never comes back on
# its own.
module Bot::Suspendable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  # Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend a bot. A delivery that gets a 2xx resets the count.
  FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT = 10

  REASONS = {
    flooding: "It posted too many messages too fast, and kept posting during its cooldown.",
    failing_webhook: "Its webhook failed #{FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT} times in a row."
  }.freeze

  included do
    scope :not_suspended, -> { where(suspended_at: nil) }
  end

  def suspended?
    suspended_at.present?
  end

  def suspension_reason_text
    REASONS[suspension_reason&.to_sym]
  end

  def suspend!(reason)
    update!(suspended_at: Time.current, suspension_reason: reason.to_s)
    Rails.logger.warn "Bot #{id} suspended: #{reason}"
  end

  # Clears the suspension along with the counts that led to it, so the bot starts afresh.
  def reactivate!
    update!(suspended_at: nil, suspension_reason: nil, consecutive_webhook_failures: 0, cooldown_until: nil, cooldown_attempts: 0)
  end

  # Locks the bot so the count is read and written against its latest state.
  def record_webhook_success
    with_lock { update!(consecutive_webhook_failures: 0) }
  end

  def record_webhook_failure
    with_lock do
      update!(consecutive_webhook_failures: consecutive_webhook_failures + 1)

      suspend!(:failing_webhook) if consecutive_webhook_failures >= FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT && !suspended?
    end
  end
end
EOF

messages.content: Next is the flood throttle. This is the core of the rate-limit rules, so I'll keep it small and make the refusal semantics explicit.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > app/models/bot/throttle.rb <<'EOF'
# Stops a bot that floods a room. A bot may post at most MESSAGES messages in any WINDOW, and messages from the message
# API and from webhook replies count alike. The message that goes over the limit is refused and starts a COOLDOWN. Every
# attempt to post during the cooldown is refused too, and the ATTEMPTS-th of them suspends the bot.
#
# The limits are fixed in code. A refusal is raised only after the bot's state is saved, so a refused attempt still
# counts. The bot is locked for the whole check and post, so two requests can't both pass the count.
class Bot::Throttle
  MESSAGES = 10
  WINDOW = 10.seconds
  COOLDOWN = 30.seconds
  ATTEMPTS = 5

  attr_reader :bot

  def initialize(bot)
    @bot = bot
  end

  # Yields to create the message if the bot may post now, and returns what the block returns. Otherwise raises
  # Bot::Suspended, or Bot::CoolingDown with the seconds left.
  def post
    refusal = nil
    message = nil

    bot.with_lock do
      refusal = refuse_attempt
      message = yield unless refusal
    end

    raise refusal if refusal

    message
  end

  private
    # Returns the refusal for this attempt, after recording the attempt, or nil when the bot may post.
    def refuse_attempt
      if bot.suspended?
        Bot::Suspended.new
      elsif cooling_down?
        attempt_during_cooldown
      elsif flooding?
        start_cooldown
      end
    end

    def cooling_down?
      bot.cooldown_until&.future?
    end

    # Counted from the messages themselves, so the window includes every message the bot has posted, and a message
    # counts whether it came from the API or a webhook.
    def flooding?
      bot.user.messages.where(created_at: WINDOW.ago..).count >= MESSAGES
    end

    def start_cooldown
      bot.update!(cooldown_until: COOLDOWN.from_now, cooldown_attempts: 0)

      Bot::CoolingDown.new(retry_after)
    end

    # next attempt is refused as a suspension.
    def attempt_during_cooldown

      bot.suspend!(:flooding) if bot.cooldown_attempts >= ATTEMPTS

      Bot::CoolingDown.new(retry_after)
    end

    # Whole seconds left, rounded up, so that a client waiting this long is let in.
    def retry_after
      (bot.cooldown_until - Time.current).ceil

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "# Stops a bot that floods a room. A bot may post at most MESSAGES messages in any WINDOW, and messages from the message
# API and from webhook replies count alike. The message that goes over the limit is refused and starts a COOLDOWN. Every
# attempt to post during the cooldown is refused too, and the ATTEMPTS-th of them suspends the bot.
#
# The limits are fixed in code. A refusal is raised only after the bot's state is saved, so a refused attempt still
# counts. The bot is locked for the whole check and post, so two requests can't both pass the count.
class Bot::Throttle
  MESSAGES = 10
  WINDOW = 10.seconds
  COOLDOWN = 30.seconds
  ATTEMPTS = 5

  attr_reader :bot

  def initialize(bot)
    @bot = bot
  end

  # Yields to create the message if the bot may post now, and returns what the block returns. Otherwise raises
  # Bot::Suspended, or Bot::CoolingDown with the seconds left.
  def post
    refusal = nil
    message = nil

    bot.with_lock do
      refusal = refuse_attempt
      message = yield unless refusal
    end

    raise refusal if refusal

    message
  end

  private
    # Returns the refusal for this attempt, after recording the attempt, or nil when the bot may post.
    def refuse_attempt
      if bot.suspended?
        Bot::Suspended.new
      elsif cooling_down?
        attempt_during_cooldown
      elsif flooding?
        start_cooldown
      end
    end

    def cooling_down?
      bot.cooldown_until&.future?
    end

    # Counted from the messages themselves, so the window includes every message the bot has posted, and a message
    # counts whether it came from the API or a webhook. A message counts while it's less than WINDOW old.
    def flooding?
      bot.user.messages.where("messages.created_at > ?", WINDOW.ago).count >= MESSAGES
    end

    def start_cooldown
      bot.update!(cooldown_until: COOLDOWN.from_now, cooldown_attempts: 0)

      Bot::CoolingDown.new(retry_after)
    end

    # The attempt that reaches ATTEMPTS is still refused with the cooldown. The bot is suspended from then on, so the
    # next attempt is refused as a suspension.
    def attempt_during_cooldown
      bot.update!(cooldown_attempts: bot.cooldown_attempts + 1)
      bot.suspend!(:flooding) if bot.cooldown_attempts >= ATTEMPTS

      Bot::CoolingDown.new(retry_after)
    end

    # Whole seconds left, rounded up, so that a client waiting this long is let in.
    def retry_after
      (bot.cooldown_until - Time.current).ceil
    end
end

  # Bot::Suspended, or Bot::CoolingDown with the seconds left.
  def post
    refusal = nil
    message = nil

    bot.with_lock do
      refusal = refuse_attempt
      message = yield unless refusal
    end

    raise refusal if refusal

    message
  end

  private
    # Returns the refusal for this attempt, after recording the attempt, or nil when the bot may post.
    def refuse_attempt
      if bot.suspended?
        Bot::Suspended.new
      elsif cooling_down?
        attempt_during_cooldown
      elsif flooding?
        start_cooldown
      end
    end

    def cooling_down?
      bot.cooldown_until&.future?
    end

    # Counted from the messages themselves, so the window includes every message the bot has posted, and a message
    # counts whether it came from the API or a webhook. A message counts while it's less than WINDOW old.
    def flooding?
      bot.user.messages.where("messages.created_at > ?", WINDOW.ago).count >= MESSAGES
    end

    def start_cooldown
      bot.update!(cooldown_until: COOLDOWN.from_now, cooldown_attempts: 0)

      Bot::CoolingDown.new(retry_after)
    end

    # The attempt that reaches ATTEMPTS is still refused with the cooldown. The bot is suspended from then on, so the
    # next attempt is refused as a suspension.
    def attempt_during_cooldown
      bot.update!(cooldown_attempts: bot.cooldown_attempts + 1)
      bot.suspend!(:flooding) if bot.cooldown_attempts >= ATTEMPTS

      Bot::CoolingDown.new(retry_after)
    end

    # Whole seconds left, rounded up, so that a client waiting this long is let in.
    def retry_after
      (bot.cooldown_until - Time.current).ceil
    end
end

## Stopping misbehaving bots

A bot that floods a room, or whose webhook keeps failing, is suspended automatically. The limits below are fixed in
code. They have no settings.

**Flooding.** A bot may post at most 10 messages in any 10 seconds. Messages posted through the message endpoint and
webhook replies both count, across all of the bot's rooms. A message counts while it's less than 10 seconds old.

- The message that goes over the limit is refused. The endpoint answers `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` set
  to the whole seconds left, and a webhook reply isn't posted. The refusal starts a 30-second cooldown.
- During the cooldown, every attempt to post is refused the same way, with the seconds left. Each such attempt counts,
  and the fifth attempt during one cooldown suspends the bot. That fifth attempt still gets `429`. From then on the bot
  gets `403`.
- Attempts during a cooldown don't extend it. Each cooldown counts its attempts from zero.

**Failing webhooks.** A delivery fails when the webhook answers with anything other than `2xx`, when it times out, or
when it can't be connected to. That includes an address refused for being private. Ten failed deliveries in a row
suspend the bot. A delivery that gets a `2xx` resets the count, whether or not the answer is posted.

**Suspended bots.**

- The posting endpoint answers `403 Forbidden`, for any room and any body.
- The bot gets no webhooks: no mentions and no joined events. A job queued before the suspension is dropped when it
  runs.
- Its rooms, memberships and messages stay as they are, and it still counts towards its owner's bot limit.
- The bots page keeps it listed, with **Suspended** and the reason, for example "Suspended: Its webhook failed 10 times
  in a row." Its creator sees this too, but can't reactivate it.
- Only administrators can reactivate it. On `/bots`, an administrator clicks **Reactivate** and confirms. Reactivation
  clears the suspension, the failure count and any cooldown. Nothing reactivates a bot on its own, and editing a bot
  doesn't reactivate it.

## Design notes

EOF

cat > 1.new <<'EOF'
**Authorization.** Editing and deleting use `Current.user.can_administer?(bot)`, which means administrator or
creator, the same rule used for other records here. Reactivating is administrators only (`Bots::ReactivationsController`,
`POST /bots/:id/reactivation`).

**Suspension and flood control.** The state lives on the `bots` row: `suspended_at` and `suspension_reason`
(`flooding` or `failing_webhook`), `consecutive_webhook_failures`, and `cooldown_until` with `cooldown_attempts`.
`Bot::Suspendable` holds the suspension, the reasons and the failure count. `Bot::Throttle` holds the flood rules.
`Bot#post_html` is the only way a bot's message is created, and it always goes through the throttle, so the API and
webhook replies are limited the same way.

- The window is counted from the bot's own `messages` rows, not from a log of posts kept alongside them. A message is
  already the record of a post, so the two can't disagree. The cost: an administrator who deletes a message removes it
  from the count.
- The check, the cooldown bookkeeping and the insert run inside `bot.with_lock`. The app's SQLite transactions start in
  immediate mode, so the lock serializes a bot's concurrent posts, and two requests can't both pass the count.
- A refusal is raised only after the transaction commits. The cooldown, the attempt count and a suspension are saved
  even though the message isn't, so a refused attempt is still counted. Raising inside the transaction would roll them
  back.
- The posting endpoint checks suspension before it looks up the room, so a suspended bot gets `403` in any room. The
  throttle checks it again under the lock, for a suspension that happens during the request.
- Webhook outcomes are recorded in `Bot::Webhook#ask_webhook`: a 2xx after the response is read, or a failure in the
  rescue. Both go through `with_lock`, so the count is read and written against the latest state.
- Suspended bots are left out before a job is queued (`Bot.receiving_webhooks`, used for mentions and joined events).
  `Bot::Webhook#deliverable?` checks again when the job runs, because the state can change while it waits.
- Refusals are `Bot::Suspended` (403) and `Bot::CoolingDown`, which carries `retry_after` for the 429 and its
  `Retry-After` header. A webhook reply that's refused is logged at info level, without its text.
- The limits are constants: `Bot::Throttle` (`MESSAGES`, `WINDOW`, `COOLDOWN`, `ATTEMPTS`) and
  `Bot::Suspendable::FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT`. Nothing in settings changes them.

## Protecting bot codes

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "# A suspended bot can't post and gets no webhooks, but it keeps its rooms and messages, and it still counts towards its
# owner's bot limit. Suspension comes from flooding (see Bot::Throttle) or from a webhook that keeps failing, which is
# counted here. Only administrators reactivate a bot (see Bots::ReactivationsController), so a bot never comes back on
# its own.
module Bot::Suspendable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  # Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend a bot. A delivery that gets a 2xx resets the count.
  FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT = 10

  REASONS = {
    flooding: "It posted too many messages too fast, and kept posting during its cooldown.",
    failing_webhook: "Its webhook failed #{FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT} times in a row."
  }.freeze

  included do
    scope :not_suspended, -> { where(suspended_at: nil) }
  end

  def suspended?
    suspended_at.present?
  end

  def suspension_reason_text
    REASONS[suspension_reason&.to_sym]
  end

  def suspend!(reason)
    update!(suspended_at: Time.current, suspension_reason: reason.to_s)
    Rails.logger.warn "Bot #{id} suspended: #{reason}"
  end

  # Clears the suspension along with the counts that led to it, so the bot starts afresh.
  def reactivate!
    update!(suspended_at: nil, suspension_reason: nil, consecutive_webhook_failures: 0, cooldown_until: nil, cooldown_attempts: 0)
  end

  # Locks the bot so the count is read and written against its latest state.
  def record_webhook_success
    with_lock { update!(consecutive_webhook_failures: 0) }
  end

  def record_webhook_failure
    with_lock do
      update!(consecutive_webhook_failures: consecutive_webhook_failures + 1)

      suspend!(:failing_webhook) if consecutive_webhook_failures >= FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT && !suspended?
    end
  end
end

# A bot that floods a room or whose webhook keeps failing is suspended (see Bot::Suspendable and Bot::Throttle).
class Bot < ApplicationRecord
  include Suspendable

  has_secure_token :bot_key

  # Raised when a bot may not post because it's suspended. The posting endpoint answers 403 Forbidden.
  class Suspended < StandardError; end

  # Raised when a bot may not post because it's cooling down after flooding. The posting endpoint answers 429 Too Many
  # Requests, with retry_after as the Retry-After header.
  class CoolingDown < StandardError
    attr_reader :retry_after

    def initialize(retry_after)
      @retry_after = retry_after
      super("Cooling down for #{retry_after} more seconds")
    end
  end

# A suspended bot can't post and gets no webhooks, but it keeps its rooms and messages, and it still counts towards its
# owner's bot limit. Suspension comes from flooding (see Bot::Throttle) or from a webhook that keeps failing, which is
# counted here. Only administrators reactivate a bot (see Bots::ReactivationsController), so a bot never comes back on
# its own.
module Bot::Suspendable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  # Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend a bot. A delivery that gets a 2xx resets the count.
  FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT = 10

  REASONS = {
    flooding: "It posted too many messages too fast, and kept posting during its cooldown.",
    failing_webhook: "Its webhook failed #{FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT} times in a row."
  }.freeze

  included do
    scope :not_suspended, -> { where(suspended_at: nil) }
  end

  def suspended?
    suspended_at.present?
  end

  def suspension_reason_text
    REASONS[suspension_reason&.to_sym]
  end

  def suspend!(reason)
    update!(suspended_at: Time.current, suspension_reason: reason.to_s)
    Rails.logger.warn "Bot #{id} suspended: #{reason}"
  end

  # Clears the suspension along with the counts that led to it, so the bot starts afresh.
  def reactivate!
    update!(suspended_at: nil, suspension_reason: nil, consecutive_webhook_failures: 0, cooldown_until: nil, cooldown_attempts: 0)
  end

  # Locks the bot so the count is read and written against its latest state.
  def record_webhook_success
    with_lock { update!(consecutive_webhook_failures: 0) }
  end

  def record_webhook_failure
    with_lock do
      update!(consecutive_webhook_failures: consecutive_webhook_failures + 1)

      suspend!(:failing_webhook) if consecutive_webhook_failures >= FAILED_DELIVERY_LIMIT && !suspended?
    end
  end
end

#
# A bot that floods a room or whose webhook keeps failing is suspended (see Bot::Suspendable and Bot::Throttle).
class Bot < ApplicationRecord
  include Suspendable

  has_secure_token :bot_key

  # Raised when a bot may not post because it's suspended. The posting endpoint answers 403 Forbidden.
  class Suspended < StandardError; end

  # Raised when a bot may not post because it's cooling down after flooding. The posting endpoint answers 429 Too Many
  # Requests, with retry_after as the Retry-After header.
  class CoolingDown < StandardError
    attr_reader :retry_after

    def initialize(retry_after)
      @retry_after = retry_after
      super("Cooling down for #{retry_after} more seconds")
    end
  end

messages.content: Found a real bug. After `reactivate!`, the database still says suspended, and the stale copy's `update!` wrote nothing. Rails' partial writes only send changed attributes, and this stale copy still believed `suspended_at` was `nil` and the failure count was `0`, so setting them to those values looked like no change. The controller loads a fresh record, so the admin path would have worked, but any caller holding an older copy would silently fail. Every other state write in this design goes through `with_lock`, which reloads first, so `reactivate!` should too. I'll fix it and add a regression test for the stale-copy case.

messages.content: That explains it, and it's the test harness, not the app. `perform_enqueued_jobs` with no block flushes a snapshot of the queue, so a job enqueued by another job during the flush waits for the next flush. Production queues (Resque) don't behave that way, so I'll flush twice per message in the scratch test: once for the mention job and once for the webhook job it enqueues. I'll also print the exact request count to confirm there are exactly ten deliveries before suspension.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > test/models/zz_e2e_scratch_test.rb <<'EOF' require "test_helper" class ZzE2eScratchTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase include ActiveJob::TestHelper # A mention enqueues an ask job, which enqueues a webhook job. The test helper flushes a snapshot of the queue, so the # webhook job needs a second flush. def deliver_mention(room, bot, text) Message.create!(room: room, creator: users(:jason), body: "
#{mention_attachment_for(bot.user)} #{text}
") 2.times { perform_enqueued_jobs } end test "ten failing mentions suspend the bot, and reactivation restores replies" do RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.stubs(:resolve).returns("93.184.216.34") url = "https://hooks.example.com/deploy" bot = Bot.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:david), webhook_url: url, join_all_open_rooms: true) room = rooms(:hq) stub_request(:post, url).to_return(status: 500, body: "nope") 9.times { |i| deliver_mention(room, bot, "run #{i}") } assert_not Bot.find(bot.id).suspended? assert_equal 9, Bot.find(bot.id).consecutive_webhook_failures deliver_mention(room, bot, "run 9") assert Bot.find(bot.id).suspended? assert_requested :post, url, times: 10 puts "\nE2E: 10 failed deliveries -> suspended, reason=#{Bot.find(bot.id).suspension_reason}" deliver_mention(room, bot, "while suspended") assert_requested :post, url, times: 10 puts "E2E: mention while suspended -> no 11th request" bot.reactivate! # held copy, loaded before the suspension stub_request(:post, url).to_return(status: 200, headers: { "Content-Type" => "text/plain" }, body: "Back online") deliver_mention(room, bot, "hi") assert_equal "Back online", room.messages.ordered.last.plain_text_body assert_requested :post, url, times: 11 puts "E2E: after reactivation the reply is posted: #{room.messages.ordered.last.plain_text_body.inspect}" end end EOF timeout 300 bin/rails test test/models/zz_e2e_scratch_test.rb 2>&1 | grep -E "E2E|Failure|Expected|Actual|runs,|Error" ; rm -f test/models/zz_e2e_scratch_test.rb; ls test/models | grep -c zz

# The bot message API. A bot posts by sending the message text as the raw request body, e.g.
#
#   curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-key>/messages
#
# There is no session here: the bot key in the path is the credential.
class Bots::MessagesController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access
  skip_forgery_protection

  before_action :set_bot, :ensure_not_suspended, :set_room

  rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound do
    head :not_found
  end

  # Refused while the bot is suspended, or cooling down after flooding. Retry-After is the number of seconds left.
  rescue_from Bot::Suspended do
    head :forbidden
  end

  rescue_from Bot::CoolingDown do |error|
    response.headers["Retry-After"] = error.retry_after.to_s
    head :too_many_requests
  end

  def create
    text = message_text
    return head :unprocessable_content unless text

    @message = @bot.post_text(@room, text)

    head :created, location: message_path(@message)
  end

  # Clients send curl's default form encoding, and Rails would try to parse the body as form fields before the
  # action runs, rejecting text such as "100% done". The body is the message, so it's never read as fields.
  def process_action(...)
    request.request_parameters = {}
    super
  end

  private
    def set_bot
      @bot = Bot.active.find_by(bot_key: params[:bot_key])

      unless @bot
        response.headers["WWW-Authenticate"] = %(Bot realm="Campfire")
        head :unauthorized
      end
    end
# Administrators decide when a suspended bot comes back. Members see that a bot is suspended, but can't reactivate it.
class Bots::ReactivationsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :ensure_can_administer

  def create
    Bot.find(params[:bot_id]).reactivate!

    redirect_to bots_url
  end
end

messages.content:
Flood and webhook-failure suspension are in place, with admin-only reactivation on the bots page. The full suite passes (542 runs, 0 failures, 22 pre-existing DNS skips), and rubocop and brakeman are clean. I could not run the browser system tests because chromedriver can't be installed offline, so the Reactivate confirm flow is verified at the markup level only.

**What changed**
- **Flooding:** `Bot::Throttle` enforces 10 messages per 10 seconds, counted from the bot's own message rows across all its rooms. The 11th post gets `429` with `Retry-After`, starts a 30-second cooldown, and webhook replies are not posted. Five attempts during one cooldown suspend the bot.
- **Failing webhooks:** `Bot::Webhook` counts any non-2xx, timeout, or connection error as a failed delivery. Ten in a row suspend the bot, and any 2xx resets the count.
- **Suspended bots:** the posting endpoint returns `403`, no webhooks are queued or sent, and the bot keeps its rooms, messages, and place in its owner's limit. The bots page shows "Suspended" with the reason.
- **Reactivation:** `POST /bots/:id/reactivation`, admin-only, with a "Reactivate" button that uses `data-turbo-confirm` (the native `confirm()`).
- **State:** a migration adds suspension, cooldown, and failure-count columns to `bots`. The limits are constants in code.
- **Docs:** `docs/bots.md` has a new "Stopping misbehaving bots" section, design notes, and updated posting and webhook tables.

**Decisions you may want to check**
- The fifth attempt during a cooldown gets `429`, and every attempt after that gets `403`. I read "responds with 429 during the cooldown" as covering that attempt.
- Webhook replies refused during a cooldown count as attempts toward the five.
- Mentions and `joined` events both count as deliveries. A bot created with "join all open rooms" and a failing webhook therefore starts with two failures.
- A refused private or internal webhook address counts as a failed delivery.

**Bug found and fixed during testing:** `reactivate!` on a copy of the bot loaded before the suspension silently wrote nothing, because Rails only saves changed attributes. It now runs under the same lock as the other state writes, and a regression test covers it. The controller loads a fresh record, so the admin path worked either way.

**Tests:** 61 new tests across the throttle, suspension, webhook delivery, posting endpoint, reactivation, bots page, and enqueue exclusion. I also checked the full path (mention → job → failures → suspension → reactivation → reply) with a scratch test and then removed it.
